title: microburst throttle trace notes
content:
Context / symptom:
- Production traffic showed recurring short-duration throughput collapses (~10-30s) where tokens/sec drops by 60-80% while request rate stays flat. P50 latency increases marginally but P95/P99 spikes dramatically. Looks like many requests are being sent as tiny batches (1-3 requests) and queuing delays + cold-KV misses amplify cost.

What I observed (raw):
- Top-level metric: aggregate tokens/s from 10:14:20 to 10:14:50 dropped from 45k -> 8k.
- Concurrent inflight requests roughly unchanged (350 -> 330).
- Batcher window occupancy shows lots of small flushes (size 1-2) at same time as large flush gaps.

Quick hypotheses:
1) Batcher misconfigured: BATCH_MAX_WAIT_MS or BATCH_MIN_SIZE reset by rollout config; a new default introduced (auto-tune) causing too aggressive flush for latency SLOs.
2) Smart routing sends small requests to dedicated nodes with busy GPU util causing thrashing and cross-AZ egress.
3) KV cache prefetch/backpressure: cache miss storm causes blocking on IO path, leading to small KV fill latencies that keep batches small.
4) Autoscaler flapping: new pods come up with cold caches and consistent tiny-batch routing until warm.
5) A race in continuous-batcher when windowed timer is re-armed incorrectly under certain CPU-load patterns.

Commands & shards of evidence tried so far (timestamps are local):
- Grabbed k8s logs for batcher pods around incident windows:
  kubectl -n inference logs pod/batcher-7f9dc --since=1h | sed -n '1,200p'
  -> repeated entries: "flush window expired, size=1, wait_ms=EXHAUSTED" and occasional "timer rearm failed: already-closed"

- API-level reproduction sniffing:
  for i in `seq 1 500`; do curl -sS -X POST https://api.redwood/complete -d '{"prompt":"short"}' & done
  -> locally could repro small-batch flushes when client ramped in stepy bursts (burst size 8 every 100ms).

- Collected batcher internal metrics via /metrics endpoint:
  batcher.flushes.total: 8123
  batcher.flushes.size_histogram: buckets: 1:512, 2:312, 4:120, 8:40, 16+:8
  batcher.timer.active_reshuffle: 0.13
  kv.prefetch.miss_rate: 0.62 (spikes during collapse)

- pprof CPU profile during spike (10s sampling): saved as s3://redwood-debug/profiles/batcher/2026-03-08-cpu.pb.gz
  quick look: heavy time in time.Sleep + runtime.select (timer) + atomic ops inside batcher.go:queueFlushIfNeeded

- Kernel / network checks: no packet loss; pod host CPU not saturated (40-60%).

Error snippets copied from pod logs:
- [2026-03-08T10:14:23Z] WARN batcher: flush window expired but pending=1, reason=timer-expire
- [2026-03-08T10:14:23Z] ERROR kvclient: prefetch timeout (200ms) for key=model/gs:cache:12345
- [2026-03-08T10:14:24Z] INFO router: route chosen=cost-first, candidate_count=5, selected=pool-eu-west-2-b-4
- [2026-03-08T10:14:24Z] DEBUG scheduler: nodeAffinity check failed -> fallback route chosen

Interesting wiring between subsystems:
- Router sometimes chooses cost-first during midday traffic (metrics show cost-first increases just before collapse).
- Cost-first choice maps to a pool with lower reserved capacity but higher cross-traffic; that pool has a slightly higher KV miss rate.
- Batcher metrics show timer-triggered flushes dominate during these intervals, not max-size-triggered flushes.

Reproduction steps I used locally (notes):
- Synthetic client that emits 50 qps but in bursts: burst_size and interburst_ms knobs. With burst_size=6 and interburst_ms=120 we see tiny flushes. Increasing interburst_ms to 300 lets batches grow to 8-12.
- Reproducer also toggled BATCH_MAX_WAIT_MS between 10ms and 40ms. At 10ms small flushes dominate.
- When I disabled KV prefetch in the local batcher, the tiny-flush pattern still appeared but prefetch miss rate stopped spiking — suggests prefetch exacerbates but not root cause.

Notes on suspected bug in batcher timer behavior (sketch):
- Code path: incoming request increments pendingCount -> if pendingCount >= minBatch -> attempt flush immediate; else ensure timer exists.
- Hypothesis: under frequent cancellation/timeout paths (client disconnects or router latency), timer rearm can race with a concurrent cancel path, causing timer to be reset to a very small residual duration instead of full window. That produces a cluster of tiny flushes.
- pprof showing many sleeps/selects suggests timers being created/destroyed frequently. Atomic CAS in ensureTimer might be failing under contention and falling back to a default of 1ms.

Short-term mitigations tried (and effects):
- Force routing to latency-first for the impacted traffic class -> immediate reduction in tiny flushes (p50 tokens/s recovered), but cost increased (selected pools are higher-cost).
- Increased BATCH_MIN_SIZE from 2 -> 6 via runtime flag on one canary -> small-flushes eliminated on that canary; latency for single-request callers degraded for that canary.
- Disabled KV prefetch for one pool -> reduced I/O stalls and smoothed batch sizes slightly.
- Restarted batcher pods to clear any timer state -> transient improvement for 90s then recurrence.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Is there a release that touched batcher timer logic around 2026-02? Check git history (PRs that modified EnsureTimer/Timer rearm logic).
- Are client-side retry/backoff patterns causing bursty arrival patterns? Need to check ingress LB logs and client SDK version distribution.
- Should we add stronger invariants/asserts in timer rearm path to avoid tiny residual durations?

Planned experiments (priority ordered):
1) Canary flag: set BATCH_FORCE_TIMER_RECREATE=false -> purpose: avoid re-create-only behavior, prefer reset. Measure flush size histogram.
2) Telemetry change: emit timer_duration_on_rearm and timer_creation_count to pinpoint rearm frequency.
3) Router policy A/B: lock a small percentage (5%) of traffic to latency-first for 24h to collect before/after batch histograms and cost delta.
4) Add a guard in continuous-batcher: if last_flush_size < 2 and last_flush_interval < 50ms for N times, throttle timer-triggered flushes for short penalty window.
5) Load test: simulate production 95th percentile burst patterns (from ingress traces) with replay harness to reproduce effect deterministically.

Notes for follow-up (who to ping):
- @Lina (batcher owner) to review ensureTimer race hypothesis and look at atomic CAS fallback code.
- @Nate (router) to check recent changes to cost-first weighting and pool mapping rules.
- @infra-sre to correlate autoscaler activity and pod restarts around incidents.

Useful artifacts I saved locally:
- s3://redwood-debug/traces/microburst/2026-03-08-traces.zip (k8s logs + metrics + pprof)
- perf traces: /tmp/perf-batcher-20260308.data
- simplified reproducer: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/tree/debug/microburst-reproducer (branch)

Immediate next steps I will take (today):
- Create a small PR adding timer_exptime metric and a quick assert on min rearm duration (1ms -> 10ms).
- Run the replay harness with client burst profiles sampled from production ingress (sample set attached in s3).
- Post initial findings in #CBATCH-debug with summary and attach histograms.

Random notes / scratch lines (keep):
- observed: "timer rearm failed: already-closed" -> search for exception origin in go runtime code path.
- check deadlines and context cancels in worker flow.
- consider backpressure signal from KV path to batcher (if KV slow -> make batcher wait up to Xms more to allow aggregation).

End of notes.
